title: Severe El Niño Heat Wave Could Cause Over 450,000 Deaths Worldwide, Study Warns
snippet: A stark report from the Climate Impact Lab warns that El Niño-fueled extreme heat could lead to nearly half a million additional deaths by late February, with developing nations bearing the brunt of the crisis.
content:
A brutal combination of a powerful El Niño pattern and human-driven global warming could result in nearly 450,000 additional heat-related deaths worldwide by the end of February, according to a sobering new study released Wednesday by the Climate Impact Lab.

Researchers at the University of Chicago-based initiative project that as many as 451,000 excess heat fatalities could occur compared to a typical baseline year. Spiking temperatures are already driving severe droughts, devastating wildfires, and shrinking freshwater supplies across the globe.

Global South Faces the Deadliest Toll

The report underscores a stark climate inequality: the deadliest consequences will disproportionately hit developing nations in the Global South that are already struggling with food insecurity, high energy costs, and fragile health infrastructure.

"If you’re already in a hot place, the extra couple of degrees are going to be much more dangerous," explained Michael Greenstone, co-founder of the Climate Impact Lab and co-author of the study. Greenstone noted that wealthier countries benefit from widespread air conditioning, dependable water grids, and robust public health systems, whereas hotter, lower-income regions lack these critical lifelines.

The study identifies Africa's semi-arid Sahel region as the hardest-hit zone, with an estimated 66,800 additional deaths tied to El Niño heat. Other severe hot spots include South and Southeast Asia—with roughly 19,400 excess deaths expected across the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand, and Cambodia, 19,300 in Indonesia, and 15,800 in India—along with Latin America, where Brazil alone could see 13,300 fatalities.

A Call for Urgent Action

Despite the staggering projections, experts emphasize that thousands of lives can still be saved if governments move swiftly. The study outlines actionable interventions, including implementing early heat-warning systems, opening public cooling centers, setting up hydration stations, protecting outdoor laborers, and expanding emergency medical capacity.

Abhiyant Tiwari, a heat resilience expert at NRDC India who was not involved in the research, urged officials to view the report as a vital blueprint rather than a reason for panic. "The real measure of our preparedness is not how many heat warnings we issue, but how effectively we protect people and reduce preventable deaths," Tiwari said.

Because global land temperatures during this El Niño are expected to run about 2.1°F (1.2°C) higher than normal—yielding 44% more extremely hot days—scientists warn that this event offers a terrifying window into average climate conditions expected 20 years from now, giving world leaders a crucial opportunity to build resilience today.
